extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism, classical aesthetics, and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Aristotle's evaluative principles for poetry, music, dance, and the plastic arts — focusing on imitation (μίμησις), rhythm, medium, and the aim of art as the expression of the universal/ideal. Useful for analyzing or producing literary and performative works in light of classical aesthetic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music has an ethical quality even apart from words
rubrics_metrics.description: “Melody even apart from words has an ethical quality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle and his school held that music (melody, rhythm) can directly influence moral character and emotions without verbal content. The dominant element in Greek music was rhythm; the spirit and meaning of a composition were felt to reside especially in rhythm. Use of melody and rhythm should be judged by their capacity to move the sensibility and affect character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and melodic movement imitate the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: “The external movements of rhythmical sound bear a close resemblance to the movements of the soul. Each single note is felt as an inward agitation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhythmical succession, governed by melody and rhythm laws, correspond to πράξεις (outward activities) expressive of mental states. Effective musical/rhythmic writing shows affinity with inner life, reproducing moral/psychological movements; this is the theoretic basis for music’s unique imitative capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch and scale variations convey temper and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: “A change of key affects us...like a change of colour or of movement...in the rise and fall of the pitch, Greek music possessed...a range of expression to which there is no modern parallel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical expression should exploit pitch/key and subtle intervallic scales to index temper/emotion. The text praises multiplicity of ancient scales and modulation as means to reproduce speaking-voice inflections; modern music’s relative loss of such resources is noted as diminishing direct expressive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting and sculpture convey moral/spiritual facts by signs (inferiorly to music)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Painting and sculpture directly render little more than the outward and physical features of an object, and...convey moral and spiritual facts almost wholly by signs or symbols...form and colour are ‘rather signs of moral qualities.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual arts should be evaluated as using form, line, and colour to suggest moral/inner qualities indirectly. They are less immediate in conveying moral life than music; their symbolism and conventional associations are central to their expressive success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial expression and gesture are natural, living signs of character
rubrics_metrics.description: “Facial expression, gestures, attitudes, are a dialect which nature herself has taught...They are in the truest sense a natural, not an artificial medium of expression.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing character (in drama, painting, sculpture, dance), rely on natural, instinctive bodily signs rather than arbitrary conventions. Such living signs convey meaning without conscious inference and are powerful tools for expressive realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plastic arts capture a single typical, representative moment
rubrics_metrics.description: “Painting and sculpture...fix eternally the feeling they portray. A single typical moment is seized and becomes representative of all that precedes or follows.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sculptural/ pictorial works for their success in selecting and embodying a representative moment that stands for a broader sequence of actions or states. Use of symmetry (analogous to rhythm) helps convey what motion conveys in time-based arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing imitates character, emotion, and action and must be perspicuous
rubrics_metrics.description: “Even dancing...imitates character, emotion, action...The dancer must have a fine genius, a critical judgment of poetry, a ready and comprehensive memory...Above all he needs to have mastered all mythology...He must avoid the ‘terrible solecisms’ of some ignorant performers...he should aim at being always perspicuous; he must be understood though he is dumb and heard though he says nothing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dance by its capacity to depict shades of character and emotion, the performer’s knowledge (literary/mythological), memory, critical judgment, and clarity of expression. Avoidance of technical/conventional errors (‘solecisms’) and communicative lucidity are key performance criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry’s medium is language/signs but its representation is not purely symbolic
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry...produces its effects (except such as depend on metre) through symbols alone...the representation is not purely symbolical; for the signs are those significant words which in life are the natural and familiar medium by which thought and feeling are revealed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic language should employ words that are natural carriers of thought and feeling; although poetry uses signs, these are rooted in common life and allow the representation to be direct (not merely arbitrary symbols). Evaluate diction for its naturalness and capacity to evoke images grounded in experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: The essence of poetry is imitation of the idea, not metre
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry...is a form of artistic μίμησις, and its essence lies rather in the ‘imitation’ of the idea than in the mere versification...the meaning of the word ‘poet’ should be widened so as to include any writer...whose work is an ‘imitation’ within the aesthetic meaning of the term.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging poetic works, prioritize their mimetic power — how well they imitate human action, character, and the universal idea — over formal metrical features. Prose mimes and dialogues can be poetic if they enact imitation effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre and melody are embellishments, not the essence of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: “Melody and the verse are the ‘seasoning’ of the language...They hold a place...similar to that which ‘external goods’ occupy in the Aristotelian definition of happiness. Without them a tragedy may fulfil its function, but would lack its perfect charm.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metrical form and musical setting as augmenting features that enhance poetic effect but are not constitutive of poetic quality. Evaluate their contribution to pleasure and effect, while recognizing that imitation remains primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry, music, and dancing form a triad united by rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry, music, and dancing constitute in Aristotle a group by themselves, their common element being imitation by means of rhythm—rhythm which admits of being applied to words, sounds, and the movements of the body.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cross-media works for rhythmic integration: how rhythm organizes language, sound, and movement to produce coherent imitation. Successful works exploit rhythm as a unifying expressive principle across modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should imitate the universal/ideal (τὸ βέλτιον) rather than the mere particular
rubrics_metrics.description: “Imitative art in its highest form, namely poetry, is an expression of the universal element in human life...fine art eliminates what is transient and particular and reveals the permanent and essential features of the original...Art...imitates the ideal; the creations of his art are framed on those ideal lines that nature has drawn...He produces a new thing...a βέλτιον, or higher reality—‘for the ideal type must surpass the actual.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate artworks by their success in abstracting and expressing the universal form or ideal underlying experience. The artist’s aim is to reveal permanent, essential features (the eidos) and to present an idealized ‘better’ version of reality rather than a mere copy of contingent particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitativeness is the defining property of 'fine art' (architecture excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Architecture...had not the ‘imitative’ quality which was regarded as essential to fine art...The decorative element in Greek architecture is alone ‘imitative’ in the Aristotelian sense.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: According to Aristotle’s criteria, classify arts by their imitative relation to human life: arts that imitate human actions/character (poetry, music, dance, drama, sculpture) are fine arts; arts lacking such imitation (architecture, broadly practical arts) are judged differently. This affects whether works are assessed as ‘fine’ art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic signs and images vary culturally and are not a universal language
rubrics_metrics.description: “The sign too and the thing signified are not here so linked together by obvious suggestion that their meaning is at once and everywhere apprehended; they vary with race and country, they cannot claim to be a universal language.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating poetry, consider cultural variability of symbols and images: poetic signs require interpretation and may not carry universal immediate meaning. Sensitivity to audience background and the conventionality of images is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: The balance of thought and musical sound in poetry matters (avoid empty musicalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are some lyrics which have lived...by their musical charm...We need not agree with a certain modern school who would empty all poetry of poetical thought and etherealise it till it melts into a strain of music...Aristotle comes perilously near this doctrine, and was saved...only by an instinctive reluctance to set at naught the traditional sentiment of Greece.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate lyrical writing for a balance between musical/auditory charm and substantive poetic thought or representation of the world. Excessive emphasis on sound at the expense of ideological or representational content is critiqued.
